clue.text: Hilarious performance by butcher with his cleaver

definitions.meaning: so funny it makes your sides ache with laughter

definitions.text: performance by butcher with his cleaver
definitions.meaning: a butcher's work dividing carcasses into sides of meat

explanation.definitionFit: Something hilarious is said to split your sides with laughter, while a butcher literally cleaves sides of beef apart.

clue.text: Form of transport maintenance needed in weaver's business?

definitions.meaning: a regular back-and-forth bus, train or air link
upkeep of the device that carries the weft thread across the loom

explanation.definitionFit: A regular to-and-fro transport link, and also the repair of a loom's thread carrier.

clue.text: One non-drinker in the party. Same again

indicators.note: the first pieces go inside the word for a party

parts.note: DO is a party or celebration
I is the Roman numeral one
TT, teetotal, describes someone who abstains from alcohol

explanation.surface: A teetotaller at a party orders the same as before.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means the same thing as was just said, as when repeating an order.

clue.text: Sounds like you mis-hit on course — shorten the line with this

parts.note: a ewe, which is pronounced like 'you', is a sheep
in golf a shank is a shot struck off the heel of the club

explanation.surface: A golfer's poor shot, followed by advice on cutting short a rope.
explanation.walkthrough: 'You' sounds like ewe, a female sheep, so the whole phrase stands for that animal. A sheepshank is a knot used to shorten a rope without cutting it.
explanation.definitionFit: This knot is tied to take up slack and shorten a rope without cutting it.

clue.text: Warning for one in the crow's nest

definitions.meaning: the cry telling someone to beware
the sailor posted at the masthead to watch for danger

explanation.definitionFit: A shout of 'beware', and the sentry who keeps watch from a ship's masthead.

clue.text: This night for playing — with this man in reserve?

definitions.meaning: the Shakespeare comedy that has a festive night in its title
in cricket the extra player who fields as a substitute

explanation.walkthrough: In cricket, the reserve beyond the eleven players is named by the ordinal after eleven.
explanation.definitionFit: Shakespeare's comedy is titled after the night ending Christmas festivities, and cricket's substitute fielder is the man after eleven.

clue.text: No Long Island, this

parts.note: a word that means a small isle in Scotland and also a short measure, so it is neither long nor big

explanation.walkthrough: In Scottish place names the word means a small island, as well as being a short unit of length.
explanation.definitionFit: A Scottish islet bears this name, which is also a tiny unit of length, hence nothing long.

clue.text: Boasting is what sage can do perhaps

indicators.note: the letters of these words might be rearranged into another form

explanation.surface: Bragging is what a wise man may be able to manage.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means extravagant bragging, named after Gascons, reputed to be braggarts.

clue.text: In short two scholars like this one could make a cake

definitions.text: In short two scholars like this one could make a cake

parts.words: In short two scholars like this one could make a cake
parts.note: the degree is abbreviated BA, and two of those side by side make a rum baba

explanation.definitionFit: This first university degree is shortened to BA, and doubled the letters spell a rum-soaked sponge cake.

clue.text: Standard position appears crazy

definitions.meaning: where a flag, or standard, flies: aloft on its mast
British slang for mad or badly mistaken

explanation.walkthrough: In British slang a person who is badly wrong or a bit mad is said to be up the pole.
explanation.definitionFit: A flag flies at the top of its staff, and the same phrase is British slang meaning mad or muddled.

clue.text: Killer struck about twice, without quarter

indicators.note: used in its old sense of outside, so the pair encloses the next piece
the word for about is to be written two times in a row

parts.note: CA is circa, Latin for about
S, south, is one of the four quarters of the compass

explanation.surface: A report on a murderer who stabbed twice and showed no mercy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Struck' completes the picture of the assassin: Casca was the first conspirator to stab Caesar. 'Without quarter' looks like 'mercilessly' but means a compass point outside.
explanation.definitionFit: Casca was one of the conspirators who assassinated Julius Caesar, as dramatised by Shakespeare.

clue.text: Hamlet's one — not so Porthos perhaps

indicators.note: signals that the musketeer's name is rearranged once the letters of 'so' are taken away, as 'not' asks

explanation.surface: A Danish prince compared with one of the Three Musketeers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hamlet' poses as Shakespeare's prince, set against Dumas's musketeer Porthos; it is really a small village. Take S and O ('not so') from PORTHOS and rearrange the rest.
explanation.definitionFit: Thorp is an archaic word for a village, surviving in English place names, so it names a small settlement.

clue.text: Actor fellow catches fish

indicators.note: the two words hold the fish inside them, as a net catches it

explanation.surface: An actor colleague goes angling and lands a fish.
explanation.definitionFit: The orfe is a freshwater fish related to the ide, often kept golden in ornamental ponds.

clue.text: Burns may have finished off a page of Shakespeare

definitions.meaning: a winged insect drawn to a flame is killed by burns
a pageboy character, Don Armado's servant in Love's Labour's Lost

explanation.walkthrough: 'Burns' tempts you toward the Scots poet, but here it is a verb: the creature dies in the candle flame.
explanation.definitionFit: Insects fly into candles and are killed by the heat; Shakespeare also named Armado's boy servant after the insect.

clue.text: Royal setting for Land of Hope etc

definitions.text: Royal setting for Land of Hope etc

parts.words: Royal setting for Land of Hope etc
parts.note: the London concert venue where Land of Hope and Glory is sung at the Last Night of the Proms

explanation.walkthrough: The Last Night of the Proms, a London summer concert, ends with the patriotic song Land of Hope and Glory in the Royal Albert Hall.
explanation.definitionFit: The domed Kensington concert venue, with Royal in its full title, hosts the Proms.

clue.text: We hear things in this evidence of being talked about?

definitions.meaning: the range within which sounds can be heard
burning ears, which folklore says mean someone is discussing you

explanation.definitionFit: Earshot is hearing range; split it and it reads as ears hot, the old sign that others are gossiping about you.

clue.text: Declaim about Monet's new style, with blooming repeats during the year

definitions.text: with blooming repeats during the year

indicators.note: the word for declaim goes around the rest

parts.note: to rant is to declaim loudly

indicators.note: the painter's name is given a new arrangement

parts.note: the 's only shows possession or stands for 'is', so it adds no letters: the word before it gives these letters as it is written

explanation.surface: Someone holds forth on the Impressionist's fresh manner of painting flowers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'About' puts EMONT, rearranged from MONET by 'new style', inside RANT. Remontant roses flower more than once a season.
explanation.definitionFit: Gardeners use the term for roses and other plants that flower again in the same season.

clue.text: The only item of luggage one needs?

definitions.text: The only item of luggage one needs?

parts.words: The only item of luggage one needs?
parts.note: a bag that, as its name suggests, takes everything you pack

explanation.definitionFit: A large soft travel bag is so named because it can contain everything you own.

clue.text: Judges so suited to sort out dire men

indicators.note: the two words are put into a new order, as when sorting things out

explanation.surface: Judges in court try to deal with some nasty criminals.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Suited' means dressed, not suitable: judges' robes are trimmed with white stoat fur.
explanation.definitionFit: Judges' robes were trimmed with the white winter fur of the stoat, so they were dressed in that fur.

clue.text: Blood A 1 — came out top

indicators.note: the letters emerge in a different order

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: Blood group A1 tested as best.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Top' poses as 'best' but is the spinning toy, juggled on a string between two sticks.
explanation.definitionFit: A diabolo is a two-cupped spinning toy kept whirling on a string, a kind of spinning top.

clue.text: Animals giving sound advice to Grace Darling?

indicators.note: signals that the advice is spoken and heard rather than spelt

parts.note: she famously rowed out in 1838 to rescue shipwreck survivors, so one might urge her on with 'row, dear'

explanation.surface: Wise words for a famous heroine of the Victorian lifeboats.
explanation.walkthrough: Grace Darling was a lighthouse keeper's daughter who rowed out to rescue shipwrecked sailors off Northumberland in 1838. 'Sound' looks like 'wise' but signals speech.
explanation.definitionFit: These small deer are wild creatures of European woodland.

clue.text: Like cattle up for the rodeo — in form like 14

definitions.text: Like cattle up for the rodeo
definitions.meaning: herded together, as cattle are before a rodeo
circular in shape, as the hall in 14 is

explanation.walkthrough: Cattle are rounded up; the Albert Hall at 14 is a famous round building.
explanation.definitionFit: Cattle herded together are said to be gathered up, and a circular building is curved in shape.

clue.text: "But still the -her ancient Ruby yields" (Fitzgerald)

parts.note: a line from FitzGerald's Rubaiyat of Omar Khayyam with a missing word to supply, the plant whose ruby fruit gives wine

explanation.definitionFit: In FitzGerald's verse the grape plant still yields its red wine, the ancient ruby, though Persian glories pass.

clue.text: But a new form of prohibition

indicators.note: the two words take a new shape, their letters rearranged

explanation.surface: A newly drafted ban, with reservations.
explanation.definitionFit: This is an old spelling of taboo, a ban on something forbidden by custom.

clue.text: His method is appropriate

parts.note: read 'appropriate' as the verb to take for oneself, which is how this criminal works

explanation.definitionFit: A robber's way of working is to take what belongs to others.

clue.text: Is a sort of shirt made with the French fibre

parts.note: T, as in T-shirt
LE is French for the

explanation.surface: A shirt made with a French material.
explanation.definitionFit: Istle is a plant fibre from Mexican agave, used for cord and brushes.

clue.text: One bent on being courteous

parts.note: the joint you bend when bowing or curtsying politely

explanation.definitionFit: Bending this leg joint is a gesture of respect or homage.

clue.text: 14's man keeping watch

parts.note: the hall in 14 is named after Prince Albert, and an albert is a link for a pocket watch

explanation.walkthrough: An albert is a watch chain worn across a waistcoat, named after Queen Victoria's consort; 'keeping watch' means holding the watch, not standing guard.
explanation.definitionFit: A series of linked metal rings secures a pocket watch to the waistcoat.

clue.text: Chips painting

definitions.meaning: Mr Chips, the elderly schoolmaster of James Hilton's novel Goodbye, Mr Chips
a work by a great European artist before about 1800

explanation.walkthrough: Mr Chips is the beloved veteran teacher of Hilton's novel Goodbye, Mr Chips.
explanation.definitionFit: Mr Chips is a veteran teacher, and a canvas by a great pre-modern European artist is also called this.

clue.text: Opera singers plying their trade on city thoroughfares

definitions.meaning: a Gilbert and Sullivan comic opera of 1889

definitions.text: singers plying their trade on city thoroughfares
definitions.meaning: Venetian boatmen who sing as they pole along the canals

explanation.definitionFit: Gilbert and Sullivan wrote an operetta under this title, and Venice's singing boatmen work its canal streets.
